groups.title: Sensing & mediators
groups.question: How is danger recognised and communicated?

groups.title: Immune cells
groups.question: Which cells recognise, respond and cooperate?

groups.title: Regulation & repair
groups.question: What restrains injury and shapes recovery?

groups.title: Clinical phenotypes
groups.question: Which mechanism fits this clinical context?

groups.title: Organ interfaces
groups.question: Which connections are supported by evidence?

topics.title: Pattern recognition
topics.idea: Pattern-recognition receptors detect microbial structures and damage-associated signals. They operate in immune cells and cardiac-resident cells; innate immunity is the wider system, not a separate class of signals.
topics.heart: TLRs, cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors and downstream pathways connect infection or sterile injury to inflammatory activation.
topics.evidence: Receptor expression is not proof of pathway activation. Viral and sterile injury can share sensors while requiring different interpretations.
topics.question: What is being sensed: a pathogen, damaged tissue, or both?

topics.title: Complement
topics.idea: A regulated protein cascade: classical, lectin and alternative activation converge on C3. Opsonisation, inflammatory signalling and the terminal complex are key outputs.
topics.heart: Connects host defence with tissue injury; cardiovascular research includes ischaemia–reperfusion and vascular inflammation.
topics.evidence: Mechanistic involvement does not establish benefit from complement inhibition in every cardiac disease.
topics.question: Which pathway, fragment and disease stage are implicated?

topics.title: Inflammasome
topics.idea: Intracellular protein complexes that can activate caspase-1 and promote maturation of IL-1β and IL-18.
topics.heart: A bridge between cellular danger signals and inflammatory pathways studied in cardiovascular injury.
topics.evidence: Distinguish evidence about a specific inflammasome from evidence about its downstream cytokines.
topics.question: Is the evidence about inflammasome assembly, a cytokine, or pyroptosis?

topics.title: Cytokine networks
topics.idea: Cytokines form context-dependent networks between immune, vascular and stromal cells. IL-1, IL-6 and other interleukins have distinct sources, receptors and effects.
topics.heart: Cytokine inhibition tests a specific target in a defined population; it does not test all inflammation at once.
topics.evidence: A fall in CRP or another biomarker does not establish a reduction in cardiovascular events.
topics.question: Which ligand, receptor and patient population are being studied?

topics.title: Immunometabolism
topics.idea: The interaction between metabolic state and immune-cell function.
topics.heart: Helps frame inflammatory responses to ischaemic injury and cardiometabolic stress.
topics.evidence: A promising translational field; changing a cellular metabolic pathway is not automatically a validated therapy.
topics.question: Is altered metabolism driving cell function, reflecting injury, or both?

topics.title: Gut–heart axis
topics.idea: Microbial communities and their metabolites interact with host physiology and immunity.
topics.heart: The gut–heart axis connects diet, microbial metabolism and cardiovascular phenotypes.
topics.evidence: A prospective association or a predictive model does not show that changing the microbiome prevents cardiovascular disease.
topics.question: Does the study show association, prediction or a causal intervention?

topics.title: Cardiac macrophages
topics.idea: Resident and recruited macrophage populations participate in surveillance, clearance and repair. Ontogeny, tissue niche and activation state all matter; a simple M1/M2 split is insufficient.
topics.heart: Cardiac macrophages interact with cardiomyocytes, vessels and fibroblasts. Their roles vary between homeostasis, acute injury and chronic disease.
topics.evidence: Much mechanistic evidence comes from models; origin alone does not fully define a cell’s function.
topics.question: Which origin, state, niche and time after injury?

topics.title: B & T lymphocytes
topics.idea: B and T cells mediate antigen-specific effector, memory and regulatory responses. B cells also present antigen; T-cell subsets can support injury, tolerance or repair.
topics.heart: Antigen specificity distinguishes targeted cardiac immune responses from a nonspecific inflammatory infiltrate.
topics.evidence: Cell identity, activation state and tissue context matter; “lymphocyte” is not one uniform mechanism.
topics.question: Which subset, antigen specificity and tissue compartment?

topics.title: Dendritic cells
topics.question: Which dendritic-cell subset, maturation state and antigen?
topics.idea: Dendritic cells belong to innate immunity and specialise in antigen presentation. They connect danger sensing with T-cell priming and tolerance; they do not sit outside the innate immune system.
topics.heart: Cardiac antigen sampling and presentation provide a bridge between local tissue injury, draining lymph nodes and adaptive responses.
topics.evidence: Conventional and plasmacytoid subsets have different functions. Benefits of engineered cells in experimental models do not establish a clinical treatment.

topics.title: Antigen presentation
topics.idea: Antigen-presenting cells process proteins and display peptides to T cells. Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells differ in how they prime, sustain or regulate responses.
topics.heart: Presentation of cardiac antigens links tissue injury to T-cell activation or tolerance. Antigen release alone is not evidence of pathogenic autoimmunity.
topics.evidence: Distinguish antigen presentation, demonstrable antigen-specific responses and proof that those responses cause disease.
topics.question: Who presents which antigen, through which MHC and co-signals?

topics.title: Immune tolerance
topics.idea: Mechanisms that prevent or restrain immune responses against self. Central selection and peripheral control are complementary safeguards.
topics.heart: A conceptual bridge to autoimmune disease, graft rejection and adverse effects of immune therapies.
topics.evidence: Tolerance is not simply the absence of inflammation or general immunosuppression.
topics.question: Which protective control is lost, preserved or being restored?

topics.title: Resolution
topics.idea: Active containment and ending of an inflammatory response, rather than merely a fall in inflammatory markers.
topics.heart: Timely resolution and clearance of the infiltrate are important for organised cardiac repair.
topics.evidence: Stopping inflammation and restoring functional tissue are related but different outcomes.
topics.question: Has inflammation resolved, and has tissue function recovered?

topics.title: Remodeling
topics.idea: Changes in cardiac structure and function after injury or persistent stress.
topics.heart: Inflammatory and reparative responses contribute to the trajectory after myocardial injury.
topics.evidence: Remodelling describes a process; it is not synonymous with inflammation or proof of its cause.
topics.question: Which structural change, at which phase after injury?

topics.title: Fibrosis
topics.idea: Accumulation and reorganisation of extracellular matrix, including scar formation after tissue loss.
topics.heart: A scar can preserve integrity, while persistent or diffuse fibrosis may impair function.
topics.evidence: Active fibroblast signalling, accumulated scar and potential reversibility are different quantities. An imaging signal needs validation against the biological process it is claimed to measure.
topics.question: Active fibroblast signalling, matrix deposition or established scar?

topics.title: Regeneration
topics.idea: Replacement of lost functional tissue; distinct from repair by scar formation.
topics.heart: Experimental cardiac repair studies investigate how inflammatory and stromal responses affect recovery.
topics.evidence: Results in mice do not establish restoration of human myocardium or a ready-to-use treatment.
topics.question: Is functional myocardium replaced, or is scar formation modified?

topics.title: Atherosclerosis
topics.idea: Arterial plaque disease in which lipids and inflammatory processes interact.
topics.heart: A major cardiovascular setting for studying the consequences of immune activation.
topics.evidence: Inflammation is one component of risk, alongside other established contributors.
topics.question: Does target engagement translate into fewer clinical events?

topics.title: Pericarditis
topics.idea: Inflammation of the pericardium, the sac surrounding the heart.
topics.heart: Shows why anatomical site, disease course and cause should be considered separately.
topics.evidence: Clinical assessment and disease-specific guidance are needed; a pathway alone does not define management.
topics.question: Which cause, inflammatory phenotype and recurrence pattern?

topics.title: Myocarditis
topics.idea: Inflammation involving the heart muscle.
topics.heart: Distinct from pericarditis, although the two may overlap.
topics.evidence: The cause, clinical presentation and evidence of tissue injury need individual assessment.
topics.question: What establishes inflammation, its cause and the risk profile?

topics.title: Sarcoidosis
topics.idea: A multisystem disease characterised by granulomatous inflammation.
topics.heart: Cardiac involvement is a distinct concern within a disease that may affect several organs.
topics.evidence: A diagnosis in one organ does not by itself define the presence or severity of cardiac involvement.
topics.question: Active inflammation, scar, or a combination of both?

topics.title: Amyloidosis
topics.idea: Misfolded proteins accumulate in tissue. Cardiac AL amyloidosis and transthyretin amyloidosis are biologically distinct entities.
topics.heart: Included at the boundary of the map: AL involves an immunoglobulin-producing clone, whereas ATTR is not primarily an immune-mediated myocarditis.
topics.evidence: AL and transthyretin amyloidosis are distinct; infiltration must not be equated with active immune inflammation.
topics.question: Which amyloid protein is demonstrated?

topics.title: Systemic diseases
topics.idea: Immune-mediated diseases may involve several organs rather than one isolated tissue.
topics.heart: Lupus, for example, can involve the heart as well as other organs.
topics.evidence: Mechanisms and organ patterns differ between diseases; extrapolation requires care.
topics.question: What is established in the heart, rather than inferred from another organ?

topics.title: Vasculitis
topics.idea: Inflammation affecting blood vessels, with manifestations depending on the vessels and organs involved.
topics.heart: Connects vascular injury with questions about the heart and other organs.
topics.evidence: The vasculitis subtype matters; a general label does not determine a patient’s organ involvement.
topics.question: Which subtype, vessel size, activity and cardiac manifestation?

topics.title: Autoinflammation
topics.idea: Disorders characterised by inappropriate activation of innate inflammatory pathways.
topics.heart: Offers a framework for understanding recurrent inflammatory syndromes and their interfaces.
topics.evidence: Autoinflammation and autoimmunity overlap in some settings but are not interchangeable terms.
topics.question: What supports an autoinflammatory rather than an infectious or autoimmune mechanism?

topics.title: Pulmonary hypertension
topics.idea: Elevated pressure in the pulmonary circulation, arising through different disease groups.
topics.heart: Connects pulmonary vascular disease with the workload of the right heart.
topics.evidence: The underlying group and cause matter; inflammation is not the sole explanation for pulmonary hypertension.
topics.question: Which haemodynamic group, and what evidence of immune involvement?

topics.title: Heart failure
topics.idea: A clinical syndrome with multiple possible causes.
topics.heart: Provides a shared clinical outcome in which vascular, myocardial and systemic processes may converge.
topics.evidence: Heart failure is not one immune disease; identifying a mechanism requires more than the syndrome label.
topics.question: Which cause and phenotype explain the immune signal?

topics.title: Cardio-oncology
topics.idea: The cardiovascular consequences of cancer and its treatments.
topics.heart: Immune therapies are an important interface, alongside other cancer-related cardiovascular effects.
topics.evidence: Risk and management depend on the treatment and clinical setting; mechanisms cannot be generalised across agents.
topics.question: Which therapy, immune lesion and competing diagnosis?

topics.title: Cardio-infectiology
topics.idea: The cardiovascular interfaces of infection, including infective endocarditis.
topics.heart: Connects pathogen, host response and cardiac tissue or device involvement.
topics.evidence: The selected influenza study combines human observations with mechanistic animal work. It does not explain every infection-related cardiac syndrome.
topics.question: What distinguishes pathogen persistence from immune-mediated damage?

topics.title: Transplantation
topics.idea: Replacement of a failing heart with a donor organ, with continuing attention to immune rejection.
topics.heart: Makes recognition of non-self and its regulation clinically tangible.
topics.evidence: Rejection, infection and graft dysfunction are distinct problems requiring specialist evaluation.
topics.question: Cellular rejection, antibody-mediated injury, infection or another graft problem?

topics.title: Ocular immunity
topics.idea: Immune-mediated and infectious inflammation of the eye; uveitis is one example.
topics.heart: A cross-organ perspective for reading multisystem inflammation, rather than a claim of a universal eye–heart mechanism.
topics.evidence: An inflammatory sign in the eye does not establish a cardiac diagnosis.
topics.question: Which ocular mechanism is demonstrated, and can it be extrapolated?

topics.title: Renal immunity
topics.idea: Immune injury in the kidney, illustrated by lupus nephritis.
topics.heart: Offers a cross-organ way to think about systemic disease and organ-specific damage.
topics.evidence: The selected human study identifies signatures in lupus nephritis. Its findings cannot diagnose cardiac involvement or establish a cardiac therapeutic target.
topics.question: Do circulating signatures reflect kidney injury, cardiac injury or systemic activity?

topics.title: Neuroimmune axis
topics.idea: Interactions between immunity and the nervous system; multiple sclerosis is a familiar example of immune-mediated damage.
topics.heart: Included as a neighbouring discipline for comparing tissue context and organ vulnerability.
topics.evidence: This conceptual connection does not imply a common cardiac mechanism or treatment.
topics.question: Which neural circuit, immune effector and cardiac outcome are linked?

topics.title: Pulmonary immunity
topics.idea: Immune processes in the lung, including granulomatous inflammation in sarcoidosis.
topics.heart: Connects a multisystem perspective with pulmonary and cardiovascular questions.
topics.evidence: Shared inflammatory vocabulary does not mean identical organ behaviour.
topics.question: Is cardiac stress secondary to pulmonary vascular disease or direct cardiac involvement?

topics.title: Cardio-rheumatology
topics.idea: Systemic immune-mediated diseases may involve joints, skin and internal organs.
topics.heart: Lupus illustrates why cardiovascular questions belong within a wider organ assessment.
topics.evidence: Troponin indicates myocardial injury in context; assay interference and non-inflammatory causes must also be considered.
topics.question: Inflammatory injury, vascular disease, treatment effect or an analytical interference?
